title: The Holy Spirit and His Gifts
subtitle: On the one Spirit all Christians confess, and the live question of whether the miraculous gifts continue today.
triageNote: That the Spirit is God and gives gifts to the church is settled common ground. Whether the miraculous gifts continue divides Pentecostals, charismatics, and cessationist evangelicals who otherwise share the same gospel. This is a family disagreement among people who will spend eternity together. Not a line between saved and lost.
question: The Holy Spirit is fully God, the third person of the Trinity. He convicts the world of sin, regenerates the dead heart, indwells every believer, and sanctifies the people of God over a lifetime. Christians do not argue over any of that. The live question is narrower and sharper. Did the miraculous gifts, also called the sign gifts, gifts like speaking in tongues, prophecy, healing, and the working of miracles, continue past the first generation of the church? Or did they cease once the apostles had finished their work and the Scriptures were complete? Faithful believers who love the same Bible answer that question in three different ways.
whyItMatters:
Before the three views, a few terms. This debate is thick with them, and a new believer should never be made to feel locked out of his own family's conversation.

The Spirit regenerates, which means he gives new spiritual life to a person who was spiritually dead, the new birth Jesus described to Nicodemus. He sanctifies, which means he makes a believer progressively more like Christ over the whole course of a life. Those two works belong to every Christian without exception.

The gifts themselves are called charismata, a Greek word meaning gifts of grace, things freely given that no one earns. The sign gifts are the subset that are openly miraculous. Tongues, also called glossolalia, is speaking in a language the speaker has not learned, understood by some as human languages and by others as a prayer language given by the Spirit. Prophecy is speaking a message understood to come from God. Healing and miracles are what the words plainly say.

Why does the question matter past mere curiosity. Because it shapes what you expect when you walk into a room of praying people. It shapes whether you long for a gift or distrust it. It shapes how you read your own quiet experiences, and whether you call them the Spirit or call them nothing. Get it wrong in one direction and you may quench something God is doing. Get it wrong in the other and you may chase counterfeit fire and call confusion holy. The stakes are real. They are not the gospel itself.

positions.name: Cessationism
positions.inOneLine: The miraculous sign gifts confirmed the apostles and the giving of Scripture, finished that task, and ceased with the apostolic age.
positions.bestCase:
Hear me carefully, because I am often caricatured as the man who says the Spirit stopped working. I say no such thing. Cessationism is my view, and the word simply means that I believe the miraculous sign gifts have ceased. The Spirit still convicts, regenerates, indwells, and sanctifies with full power today. I am arguing about a narrow set of gifts, not about the Spirit himself.

Look at how the sign gifts actually function in the New Testament. They cluster around the apostles. When God was doing something genuinely new, the exodus, the prophets, the coming of Christ and his apostles, he attended it with miracles to mark it as his own. Hebrews 2 says salvation was declared by the Lord and confirmed to us by those who heard, while God bore witness by signs and wonders. The signs authenticated the messengers who carried the once for all revelation. Paul calls miracles the signs of a true apostle. The gifts were credentials for a founding generation.

And that generation laid a foundation that is, by definition, laid once. Ephesians 2 says the church is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ as the cornerstone. You do not pour a foundation in every generation. Once the apostles had finished their work and the New Testament was complete, the confirming signs had done what they were given to do. To ask for them now is to ask to relay a foundation already set in concrete.

I hold this soberly, not triumphantly. I do not deny that God still heals in answer to prayer, for he is free and he is good. I deny that there are men today with the apostolic gift of healing who can empty hospitals. I deny that the prophecies and tongues claimed in many rooms today are the same thing the New Testament describes. The honest test of the gift of prophecy in Scripture is total accuracy, because it claimed to be the word of God, and what passes for prophecy today rarely survives that test. I would rather hold a high and exacting view of these gifts than a loose one that lets anything count.

positions.name: Continuationism
positions.inOneLine: The New Testament never teaches that any gift would cease before Christ returns, so all the gifts continue and the church should earnestly desire them.
positions.bestCase:
My position is called continuationism, which means simply that I believe all the spiritual gifts continue today, the miraculous ones included. I begin where I think Scripture begins, with the plain commands. Paul tells the Corinthians to earnestly desire the higher gifts. He says do not forbid speaking in tongues. He says the one who prophesies builds up the church. These are commands to a living church, with no expiration date attached.

Show me the verse that says the sign gifts would stop when the apostles died. It is not there. The cessationist case is built by inference, by stitching together a purpose for the gifts and then arguing that the purpose expired. But the New Testament itself never draws that line. The one passage that names a stopping point, 1 Corinthians 13, says the gifts will pass away when the perfect comes, when we see face to face and know fully even as we are fully known. That is not the closing of the canon of Scripture. That is the return of Christ. Until I see him face to face, the gifts that help me know in part are exactly the gifts I still need.

As for prophecy, I do not claim it equals Scripture. I take Paul seriously when he tells the church to weigh what prophets say and to hold fast what is good. A gift that must be tested is plainly not infallible the way the Bible is. New Testament prophecy is the Spirit prompting a person with something from God that the church then examines. Understood that way, it threatens the Bible not at all, and the objection that it would add to Scripture simply dissolves.

I want to be pastoral here, because I know the abuses are real and they grieve me too. But the answer to abuse is not amputation. Paul faced a Corinthian church that was a circus of disordered gifts, and his remedy was not to shut the gifts down. It was to order them, to insist that everything be done for building up, decently and in order. He regulated what he could have forbidden. I take that as my charter. Do not quench the Spirit. Desire the gifts. Then govern them in love.

positions.name: Open but Cautious
positions.inOneLine: There is no airtight biblical case that the gifts ceased, so be open to them, but be sober about the abuses and test everything.
positions.bestCase:
I stand in the middle, and I am not ashamed of it, because I think the middle is where the evidence actually leaves an honest reader. This view is sometimes called open but cautious, and it grew up in what people named the Third Wave. The name does not matter. What matters is the posture, which is two words held together. Open. Cautious.

I am open because I have read the cessationist arguments closely and I do not find them airtight. The texts that supposedly teach the gifts ceased do not quite say it. Ephesians 2 calls the apostles and prophets a foundation, and yes, a foundation is laid once, but that argument retires the office of apostle far more clearly than it retires the gift of healing or tongues. The strongest cessationist case is a cumulative one, and a cumulative case built on inference cannot bind a conscience the way a clear command can. So I will not tell God he is no longer permitted to give a gift he gave freely before.

But I am cautious, deeply cautious, because I have also seen what the so called full continuationist enthusiasm produces when it is not governed. I have watched prophecy used to manipulate, healing claimed where no one was healed, and tongues turned into a badge that divides the mature from the immature, which is the precise error Paul was correcting in Corinth. The same Paul who said do not quench the Spirit said in the very next breath to test everything and hold fast what is good. Those two commands are one command. Openness without testing is gullibility. Testing without openness is unbelief.

So my counsel to a new believer is calm. Do not demand the spectacular and do not forbid it. Pray for the sick and leave the outcome to God. If something happens in a prayer meeting that looks like a gift, do not panic and do not swoon. Weigh it against Scripture, watch whether it builds up the body, and hold on to what proves good. I would rather be caught expecting too little of God and corrected, than be caught calling every loud thing the Holy Spirit.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Shared ground for all three views
biblicalEvidence.summary: Paul teaches that the Spirit gives a variety of gifts to the one body of Christ, distributing to each one as he wills. The list includes both the ordinary, like teaching and service, and the miraculous, like healing, miracles, prophecy, and tongues. The point of the chapter is that the body needs every part and no member may say to another that he is not needed.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: It is not sharply hard for anyone, but it presses the cessationist to explain why a chapter that treats miraculous and ordinary gifts as one undivided body would have the miraculous half quietly drop out while the rest remained.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The cessationist answers that a gift can be real and given for a founding era without being permanent, just as the office of apostle was real and is now closed. Continuationists and the open view read the chapter as describing the church's permanent endowment. Nothing hints that part of it was temporary.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Contested by all three, the central cessation text
biblicalEvidence.summary: Paul says love never ends. But as for prophecies they will pass away, as for tongues they will cease, as for knowledge it will pass away. We know in part and prophesy in part. But when the perfect comes the partial will pass away. Now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face. This is the one passage that explicitly names a time when the gifts stop.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for everyone, because everything hangs on the meaning of the phrase when the perfect comes. If the perfect is the completed Bible, the cessationist wins the verse. If the perfect is the return of Christ, the continuationist wins it.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Most cessationists today concede that the perfect most naturally means Christ's return or the final state, and so they do not rest their case here, they argue cessation on other grounds. Continuationists press exactly this point, that seeing face to face and knowing fully can only describe the world to come, so the gifts run until then. The open view agrees the text points to Christ's return and therefore declines to use it as a proof that the gifts have already stopped.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Read in support of continuation, and by Pentecostals for subsequence
biblicalEvidence.summary: At Pentecost the Spirit is poured out. The believers speak in tongues. Peter explains it by quoting the prophet Joel. In the last days God will pour out his Spirit on all flesh, and sons and daughters will prophesy. Peter says the promise is for you and your children and for all who are far off. It is for everyone whom the Lord calls.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for cessationism, because Peter frames the outpouring as a feature of the whole last days, the entire span between Christ's first and second coming, and extends the promise to those far off in later generations.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Cessationists answer that Pentecost was a unique, unrepeatable founding event, like the first Easter, and that the phrase last days describes the era inaugurated, not a guarantee that every sign recurs in every believer. Pentecostals also read the chapter as a pattern for a second experience after conversion, a point disputed below under related debates.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Paul says the church is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone. A foundation, by its nature, is laid once at the start of a building and not repeated.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for the fullest continuationism, because it suggests the apostles and a certain kind of foundational prophet had a once for all role that is not ongoing.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Cessationists take this as a clear pillar, the office of apostle and foundational prophet is closed, and they extend the principle to the sign gifts those offices carried. Continuationists answer that the verse retires the foundational office, not every gift, and that the everyday gift of prophecy Paul regulates in 1 Corinthians 14 is a different and lower thing than the foundation laying prophets here. The open view finds this the cessationist's strongest verse and grants it real weight. It still denies it proves the whole case.

biblicalEvidence.summary: The writer says this great salvation was declared at first by the Lord and was confirmed to us by those who heard him. God also bore witness by signs and wonders and various miracles and by gifts of the Holy Spirit distributed according to his will. The miracles confirmed the message carried by the first hearers.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for continuationism in its strong form, because it ties the signs tightly to the authentication of the original gospel witnesses and speaks of that confirming in the past tense.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Cessationists read it as proof that the sign gifts had a confirming purpose tied to the founding generation. That purpose is now complete. Continuationists answer that confirming the message was one purpose of the gifts but never the only one. 1 Corinthians 14 says prophecy and the rest were also given to build up the ordinary church. That need has not expired. The open view grants the confirming purpose was real and central. It declines to make it the sole purpose.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: The open but cautious anchor, claimed by continuationism
biblicalEvidence.summary: Paul writes do not quench the Spirit, do not despise prophecies, but test everything, hold fast what is good. In four short commands he both protects the gifts and disciplines them.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for a strict cessationism, because the command not to despise prophecy and to test it assumes a living congregation in which prophecy is operating and needs weighing.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Continuationists and the open view treat this as the governing posture for all the gifts. Openness and testing held together. Cessationists answer that the command applied fully to the apostolic church where prophecy was active. The duty to test everything by Scripture remains permanently. But the gift that prompted it has ceased.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Read in support of continuation and ordered use
biblicalEvidence.summary: Paul gives detailed instructions for the orderly use of tongues and prophecy in the assembly. Pursue love and earnestly desire the spiritual gifts, especially prophecy. Let tongues be interpreted. Let prophets speak in turn and let others weigh what is said. He ends, do not forbid speaking in tongues, but let all things be done decently and in order.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for cessationism, because Paul regulates these gifts rather than retiring them and issues a standing command not to forbid tongues.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Continuationists take the chapter as a permanent charter. The gifts are commanded. Only their disorder is corrected. The open view agrees. It stresses the ordering as the cure for abuse. Cessationists answer that Paul rightly regulated gifts that were genuinely present in his day. But instructions for the apostolic era do not by themselves prove the gifts persist once their confirming purpose is finished.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: The cessationist sign of an apostle text
biblicalEvidence.summary: Paul says the signs of a true apostle were performed among the Corinthians with utmost patience, with signs and wonders and mighty works. He treats miraculous signs as a mark that distinguished a genuine apostle.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for continuationism, because it associates the most spectacular signs specifically with apostolic identity, an identity continuationists agree is not ongoing.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Cessationists read it as evidence that signs and wonders were apostolic credentials. So they fade with the apostles. Continuationists answer that signs marked apostles in a heightened way without being limited to apostles. Stephen and Philip and ordinary believers in Galatians also worked miracles. The open view grants the apostolic association. But the gifts were never walled off to the apostles alone.

weighing:
What follows is the author's own tentative judgment, offered as one pastor's reading, not a test of fellowship. Weigh it as you would weigh any prophecy, against Scripture. Hold fast only what is good.

My honest reading is that the strict cessationist case proves less than it claims. Its strongest verse, Ephesians 2:20, clearly closes the office of apostle and foundational prophet. I hold that closed with both hands. But it does not by itself close the gift of healing or the lower, testable prophecy that Paul orders in 1 Corinthians 14. And the one text that names a stopping point, 1 Corinthians 13, points most naturally to seeing Christ face to face, not to the binding of the last book of the Bible. A doctrine that the gifts have ceased should rest on a verse that says so. That verse is hard to find.

Yet I cannot walk all the way over to an unguarded continuationism either. The same Paul who said do not quench the Spirit said test everything in the same breath. And the rooms that forget the second half of that command do real damage to real people. I land near the open but cautious center. I have sympathy for the continuationist reading of the texts and deep respect for the cessationist's exacting standard, especially his insistence that prophecy which claims to be from God must actually be true. I would rather expect too much of a living God and be corrected by Scripture than wall him off from his own church on an argument built of inference.

That is my judgment, held loosely, and I have watched men I admire land in all three places.
charitableDisagreement:
Notice what every one of these positions confesses together, because it dwarfs what divides them. The Holy Spirit is fully God. He convicts the sinner, raises the dead heart to new life, lives inside every believer, and conforms us to Christ across a lifetime. He gives gifts to his church. No cessationist denies the Spirit's power, and no continuationist worships a different Spirit. This is a disagreement among brothers and sisters about how one chapter of the Spirit's work runs in this present age, not a disagreement about whether the Spirit is at work.

So handle one another gently. The continuationist should not call the cessationist a man who quenches the Spirit, and the cessationist should not call the continuationist a man who chases counterfeit fire. Both are loving the same Lord and reading the same Bible with care. Is this a hill to die on. No. It is a hill to think hard on, to pray over, and to hold with an open hand. And all the while you go on receiving the Spirit who is far greater than the argument about his gifts.

relatedDebates.topic: Baptism in the Spirit and subsequence
relatedDebates.note: Classical Pentecostal teaching holds that there is a baptism in the Spirit, a distinct empowering work that comes as a second experience after conversion. It is often evidenced by speaking in tongues. The technical word for this two stage pattern is subsequence, meaning the Spirit baptism follows conversion as a separate event. The Pentecostal reads the book of Acts as a pattern. Believers are converted and then later filled. Most other evangelicals, including many charismatics and nearly all cessationists, hold instead that every believer is baptized in the Spirit at the moment of conversion. They cite 1 Corinthians 12:13, that in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body. On this reading the baptism in the Spirit is not a second blessing for some Christians but the common possession of all. The later fillings in Acts are fresh empowerings rather than a separate initiation. This debate overlaps with the gifts debate but is not identical to it, since a person can believe all the gifts continue while denying that Spirit baptism is a second experience.

Even among those who believe tongues continue, there is a further question of what tongues are. Some hold they are always real human languages, as at Pentecost, given so the gospel could be heard across the barrier of language. Others hold that the tongues Paul describes in 1 Corinthians 14, spoken to God and needing interpretation, can be a non human prayer language given by the Spirit. How a person answers this shapes what he expects tongues to sound like and how he tests a claim to the gift.
